title: Soft White Bread (Tangzhong Method)
description: A soft, pale, everyday loaf that stays tender for days without milk, butter, or yellowing — thanks to the tangzhong technique.

ingredients.notes: for tangzhong — increased to account for evaporation

method.instruction: Make the tangzhong: in a small saucepan, combine 30 g bread flour and 190 g water. Cook over medium heat, whisking constantly, until it thickens into a paste at approximately 65°C. Remove from heat and let cool to room temperature. It should weigh approximately 150–160 g after cooking.
In a large bowl, combine bread flour, salt, sugar, yeast, and bread improver.
Add the cooled tangzhong, water, and vegetable oil to the dry ingredients.
Mix until a rough dough forms, then knead for 10–12 minutes by hand or 7–8 minutes in a stand mixer until smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky but not sticky.
Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with a damp tea towel, and let rise in a warm place for 1–1½ hours until doubled in size.
Punch down the dough and shape into a loaf. Place in a greased loaf tin approximately 20 cm × 10 cm.
Cover and let rise for another 45–60 minutes until the dough has risen about 1–2 cm above the rim of the tin.
Bake for 28–32 minutes until the top is golden brown and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom.
Remove from tin immediately and cool on a wire rack for at least 30 minutes before slicing.

notes.title: Why Tangzhong Works
notes.content: The tangzhong pre-gelatinises the starch, allowing the dough to hold more moisture. This keeps the bread soft and fresh for 2–3 days without refrigeration.

notes.title: Neutral Oil for Pale Crumb
notes.content: Using vegetable oil instead of butter keeps the crumb pale white. The tangzhong locks in moisture without making the dough sticky.

notes.title: Weighing Tangzhong
notes.content: For best results, weigh your tangzhong after cooking to ensure hydration is correct. It should weigh approximately 150–160 g.
